answers.primary: A PostToolUse hook of type command, matcher "Write|Edit" (add MultiEdit/NotebookEdit), configured in the repo's checked-in .claude/settings.json or shipped in a plugin's hooks/hooks.json. The script reads tool_input.file_path from stdin JSON, exits quietly unless the path ends in .ts/.tsx, and runs the formatter on that one file.
answers.rejected_alternative: CLAUDE.md / project rules, which is what the team already has: memory text is advisory instruction to the model and is exactly what gets skipped under context pressure.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. Claude Code runs the hook process itself after every matching tool call, so the formatter runs whether or not the model remembered it.
answers.context_boundary: The hook runs as a separate OS process with its own environment, outside the model's context window; it receives the tool call JSON on stdin. Only what the hook prints back (additionalContext, or a block reason) crosses into the transcript, so a silent success costs no tokens.
answers.lifecycle: Fires immediately after each successful Write/Edit tool call, for as long as the settings file is loaded in the session. It stops applying if the hook entry is removed, if disableAllHooks is set, or in any session that does not load that settings scope.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open on the hook's own errors: a non-zero exit other than 2 is treated as a non-blocking error and the turn continues, so a broken formatter silently stops formatting. It also has a coverage hole rather than a correctness hole: edits made through Bash (sed, redirection, codemod scripts) never match Write|Edit, so for the stated requirement (nothing unformatted reaches a commit) pair it with a git pre-commit hook or CI check as the real gate.
answers.version_caveat: Use ${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR} for the script path so it resolves for every teammate. Project-scope hooks only load after the workspace is trusted, and disableAllHooks or a managed allowManagedHooksOnly policy will suppress a repo-level hook entirely.

answers.primary: permissions.deny rules in the repo's checked-in .claude/settings.json, e.g. "Read(./.env)", "Read(./.env.*)", "Read(./secrets/**)" plus matching Edit(...) deny entries. Checking that file into git is what makes every teammate inherit it on clone.
answers.rejected_alternative: A PreToolUse hook that inspects file_path and returns permissionDecision deny; it works but reimplements path matching the permission engine already does, and it can be disabled with disableAllHooks.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. Permission rules are evaluated by Claude Code before the tool executes, and deny rules apply in every permission mode including auto and bypassPermissions.
answers.context_boundary: Evaluated in-process in the session, before the tool call runs. The file contents never enter the model's context; only the denial message does, so the model learns the path exists but not what is in it.
answers.lifecycle: Applies to every matching tool call from the moment settings load until the session ends. Rules from managed, user, project and local scopes merge, and a developer's local file can add rules but a deny added here cannot be removed by a narrower allow.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed for the built-in file tools, but it is scoped to those tools only: `cat .env` or a Python script run through Bash still reads the file unless you also add Bash deny rules or sandbox denyRead. The other practical failure is silent: the path-pattern syntax (project-relative `./secrets/**` vs absolute `//path` vs `~/`) is easy to get wrong, and a wrong pattern matches nothing and reports no error.
answers.version_caveat: Deny takes precedence over ask and allow, so no allow rule can re-open these paths. Project settings only take effect after the workspace-trust prompt, and if the organization sets allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly in managed settings the repo's rules are ignored entirely.

answers.primary: A Notification hook of type command in the developer's user settings (~/.claude/settings.json), matched on the notification types that mean the session is waiting (permission_prompt and idle_prompt), invoking an OS notifier such as terminal-notifier, notify-send, or BurntToast.
answers.rejected_alternative: A PreToolUse hook that fires a toast before every gated tool call; it would alert on calls that are auto-approved and never actually block, producing constant false alarms.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. Claude Code emits the Notification event and runs the hook; the model has no part in deciding whether the alert fires.
answers.context_boundary: Runs in a separate OS process on the developer's desktop, outside the model's context. Nothing needs to cross back into the conversation, which is the point: this is a side channel to the human, not to the agent.
answers.lifecycle: Fires each time Claude Code raises a notification of the matched type, for the life of the session. It stops applying when the session ends, when the hook entry is removed, or when disableAllHooks is set.
answers.failure_mode: Purely advisory and fails open: Notification hook exit codes other than 0 are logged and ignored, so a missing notifier binary means the engineer simply never gets alerted and nothing warns them. It is also per-machine, so putting it only in user settings means a new laptop or a fresh checkout silently has no alerting.
answers.version_caveat: Matcher values are notification types (permission_prompt, idle_prompt, auth_success), so a typo matches nothing. Notifier binaries differ per OS, so a single checked-in project hook needs a platform branch; a hook JSON terminalSequence (OSC 9/777) is a lighter alternative but depends on the terminal emulator honoring it.

answers.primary: Managed settings deployed by MDM: set permissions.disableBypassPermissionsMode to "disable" in the managed-settings.json for each platform (/Library/Application Support/ClaudeCode/, /etc/claude-code/, C:\Program Files\ClaudeCode\), or via the Windows policy registry key HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\ClaudeCode, or through server-managed settings for a Team/Enterprise org.
answers.rejected_alternative: A PreToolUse hook that reads permission_mode from the hook input and denies when it is bypassPermissions; that lives in a settings file the developer can edit, so it cannot meet the "must not be liftable" requirement.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness, and specifically the settings-precedence layer: managed settings sit above command line arguments and above local, project and user settings, so neither ~/.claude nor any repo file nor a CLI flag can override the key.
answers.context_boundary: This never reaches the model at all; it is a startup-time policy check in the CLI process. The only thing the model sees is that the mode is unavailable and prompts keep appearing.
answers.lifecycle: Applied at startup and on settings reload, for every session on every managed machine. It stops applying only if the managed file or policy key is removed by the fleet administrator, or if the developer runs a build that never reads it.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed for the mode itself, but the boundary is the file's ACL, not Claude Code: a developer with local administrator rights can edit the managed file, uninstall the MDM profile, or install a private copy of the CLI, so this is a policy control on a trusted endpoint rather than a hard technical guarantee. Note also that it blocks only bypassPermissions; auto mode and dontAsk are separate modes and need disableAutoMode and their own rules if they are also out of policy.
answers.version_caveat: The value is the string "disable", not a boolean. Managed-settings sources do not merge with each other: if you also deploy server-managed settings, cached server settings replace the device-managed file, so set the key in both places. Server-managed settings require a Team or Enterprise plan.

answers.primary: A Stop hook (command type) that returns {"decision": "block", "reason": "..."} when the current turn has no recorded passing test run. Pair it with a PostToolUse hook on Bash that writes a marker file keyed by session_id/prompt_id whenever the test command exits 0, so the Stop hook checks harness-recorded evidence rather than the model's claim.
answers.rejected_alternative: A skill or CLAUDE.md rule instructing the agent to always test before finishing; that is the exact failure being designed around, since the model can forget or believe it already tested.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. Claude Code runs the Stop hook when the model tries to end the turn and refuses to let the turn end when the hook blocks.
answers.context_boundary: The hook runs out of process at the turn boundary and can read the transcript path it is handed. What crosses back is only the reason string, which is injected as feedback and makes the model keep working in the same context window.
answers.lifecycle: Triggers every time the main agent finishes responding (SubagentStop is the separate event for subagents). It stops applying when the turn legitimately satisfies the check, when the session ends, or when the hook is removed.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed, which is the desired direction, but it introduces a loop risk: the Stop hook fires again after the model responds to the block, so the script must honor the "stop hook already active" flag in its input and cap retries or the session ping-pongs forever. If the check only greps the transcript for a test command rather than a harness-written marker, the model can satisfy it by running something that merely looks like the test suite.
answers.version_caveat: Exit code 2 on Stop is equivalent to blocking and continues the conversation; other non-zero codes are non-blocking. disableAllHooks turns this off, so if the gate is mandatory it belongs in managed settings alongside allowManagedHooksOnly rather than in the repo.

answers.primary: An explicit permissions.ask rule matching pushes, e.g. "Bash(git push *)", placed in managed or project settings. Ask rules are the documented exception that still forces a human prompt in bypassPermissions mode, in auto mode, and for commands that would otherwise be auto-approved by the sandbox.
answers.rejected_alternative: A PreToolUse hook returning permissionDecision "ask"; it expresses the same intent but is removable with disableAllHooks and duplicates a guarantee the permission engine already makes for ask rules specifically.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. The permission engine resolves matching rules before the tool runs and raises the prompt itself, independent of the session's mode or the model's cooperation.
answers.context_boundary: Resolved in the session process before the Bash call executes. The model sees only that the call is pending human approval; the approval decision comes from the terminal UI, not from the conversation.
answers.lifecycle: Evaluated on every Bash tool call for the whole session, from settings load. It stops applying if the rule is removed, or in dontAsk mode where ask-matching calls are auto-denied instead of prompted, which changes halt-and-wait into halt-and-fail.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed for anything that textually matches, but the match is on the command string, so it is evasive by construction: `git -C /repo push`, a push inside a shell script or Makefile target, an alias, or a chained command may not match the prefix pattern. Treat it as a strong speed bump on the normal path, not as an unbypassable control; the remote's own branch protection is the real backstop.
answers.version_caveat: A bare Bash or Bash(*) ask rule is skipped for commands the sandbox runs, so the rule must be content-scoped to git push to survive sandbox auto-allow. Allow rules have no effect under bypassPermissions, and in auto mode broad Bash allow rules are dropped, so do not rely on allow/deny interplay here.

answers.primary: A PreToolUse hook matched on Bash that appends the full tool_input.command plus session_id, cwd and timestamp to an append-only audit log or POSTs it to a collector, paired with a PostToolUse (and PostToolUseFailure) hook on Bash to record the outcome. Deploy it through managed settings so it is present on every developer machine.
answers.rejected_alternative: OpenTelemetry export via CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY; it is the right shape for fleet-wide metrics but emits events and decisions rather than a guaranteed verbatim record of each command line.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. Claude Code invokes the hook with the literal tool input, so the record is what was actually submitted for execution rather than what the model said in prose.
answers.context_boundary: The logging process runs entirely outside the model's context; the command JSON crosses out to the hook and nothing needs to cross back. Have the hook print nothing so the transcript is unaffected and the model cannot see or shape the audit trail.
answers.lifecycle: Fires on every Bash tool call for the whole session on every machine the managed settings reach. It stops applying if the managed policy is withdrawn, or for tool calls that are not Bash.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open for compliance purposes: PostToolUse hook errors are non-blocking, so a full disk or an unreachable collector loses records without stopping the agent, and PreToolUse alone logs intent (including commands later denied). The deeper gap is depth: it captures the top-level command only, so everything a launched script or a spawned child process runs is invisible, and other tools (Write, MCP servers) are not covered.
answers.version_caveat: Put it in managed settings with allowManagedHooksOnly so a developer cannot drop it, and note disableAllHooks would otherwise kill it. HTTP-type hooks are constrained by the allowedHttpHookUrls allowlist, and if you need blocking-on-log-failure semantics you must use PreToolUse exit 2, since PostToolUse cannot stop the command.

answers.primary: A PreToolUse hook on Bash that parses the command and returns permissionDecision "allow" only for an exact normalized `aws s3 ls` (with an optional bucket/prefix argument if you want that), and "deny" for every other command whose first token is aws. The hook, not the rule engine, is what lets one narrow case through without a prompt while refusing the rest.
answers.rejected_alternative: permissions.deny "Bash(aws *)" combined with permissions.allow "Bash(aws s3 ls)"; deny takes precedence over allow, so the blanket deny swallows the carve-out and the approved command is refused too.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. The hook's decision is binding on the tool call, and unlike a rule it can implement "deny everything except this one shape" in code.
answers.context_boundary: The hook runs out of process on the command string; its permissionDecisionReason is what crosses back into the transcript, so a clear reason is what teaches the model to stop retrying aws variants.
answers.lifecycle: Evaluated before every Bash tool call, for the life of the session. It stops applying if the hook is removed or disableAllHooks is set, at which point the aws surface reverts to whatever the ordinary permission rules say.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed on anything the parser does not positively recognize, which is the right default, but it is still string-level: `sh -c 'aws iam ...'`, `aws s3 ls && aws iam list-users`, env-var prefixes, a wrapper script, or a Python boto3 call all route around a naive first-token check. Write the matcher to reject compound and quoted forms outright rather than trying to understand them, and keep a deny rule as a second layer.
answers.version_caveat: Keep the hook's deny path independent of permission mode, since it must also hold in auto and bypassPermissions sessions. If the sandbox is enabled with auto-allow, sandboxed Bash commands are approved by the sandbox boundary, so the PreToolUse hook (which still runs first) is the only thing enforcing the aws restriction there.

answers.primary: The built-in Bash sandbox: set sandbox.enabled true and declare the paths under sandbox.credentials.files with "mode": "deny" (~/.aws/credentials, ~/.ssh), or equivalently sandbox.filesystem.denyRead. Enforcement is by OS primitives (Seatbelt on macOS, bubblewrap on Linux and WSL2), so it binds every process in the sandboxed command's tree, including grandchildren.
answers.rejected_alternative: More permissions.deny Read(...) rules, which is what the team already has: those are evaluated by Claude Code for its own file tools and have no visibility into a Python interpreter's open() calls.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness, and below it the operating system. The kernel-level boundary holds regardless of what the model chose to run or what the command does once it starts, which is precisely the property permission rules lack.
answers.context_boundary: The restriction applies to the Bash subprocess tree, not to the model's context. A blocked read surfaces to the model as an ordinary permission-denied error from the script, so the secret's contents never reach the transcript.
answers.lifecycle: Applies to every sandboxed Bash command for the session, from settings load. It stops applying to commands listed in excludedCommands, to commands retried with dangerouslyDisableSandbox, and entirely if the sandbox cannot start on that platform.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open by default in the dangerous direction: if bubblewrap/socat are missing or the platform is unsupported, Claude Code warns and runs commands unsandboxed, so set sandbox.failIfUnavailable true and allowUnsandboxedCommands false to make it a hard gate. Also note the credential-file protection lives in the filesystem layer, so sandbox.filesystem.disabled turns it off, and developers can always append excludedCommands entries to run a tool outside the sandbox.
answers.version_caveat: macOS, Linux and WSL2 only; native Windows is not supported and WSL1 will not work. sandbox.credentials requires Claude Code v2.1.187 or later, and filesystem.disabled (v2.1.216+) can only be set from user, managed or --settings scopes, with managed settings taking exclusive control once they configure sandbox.filesystem or any credentials.files entry. Add allowManagedReadPathsOnly so developers cannot widen allowRead.

answers.primary: Package everything IT ships as plugins in an IT-controlled marketplace, force-enable them with enabledPlugins in managed settings, and lock the surfaces there: allowManagedHooksOnly for automation scripts, allowManagedMcpServersOnly plus allowedMcpServers/deniedMcpServers for external tool servers, strictKnownMarketplaces and blockedMarketplaces for plugin sources, and disableSideloadFlags to reject --plugin-dir, --plugin-url, --agents and --mcp-config at startup.
answers.rejected_alternative: Distributing the same components as a checked-in .claude/ directory per repo; that is trivially editable by anyone with commit access and gives no central kill switch.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness, via the managed-settings layer that outranks CLI arguments and every user/project/local settings file.
answers.context_boundary: This is load-time policy in the CLI process, resolved before any component reaches the model. What crosses into the session is only the approved set of skills, agents, hooks and MCP tools; a rejected component is simply absent, and blocked loads show up in the /plugin Errors tab rather than in the transcript.
answers.lifecycle: Evaluated at startup and on settings/plugin reload, on every session on every managed machine. It stops applying if MDM stops delivering the file or the developer runs an unmanaged installation.
answers.failure_mode: The guarantee is only partial today, and this is the important caveat to give the platform team: there is no allowManagedSkillsOnly or allowManagedAgentsOnly equivalent, so skills in .claude/skills and .claude/commands and subagent definitions in ~/.claude/agents and .claude/agents still load even under full lockdown (disableBundledSkills only removes Anthropic's own bundled ones). The hook and MCP halves fail closed; the skills and agents half has to be enforced outside Claude Code with filesystem ACLs or endpoint policy, and it fails open until then.
answers.version_caveat: disableSideloadFlags requires Claude Code v2.1.193 or later and is managed-settings-only; without it a developer can sideload with --plugin-dir and bypass strictKnownMarketplaces. Managed-settings sources do not merge, so if you also use server-managed settings the cached server copy replaces the MDM file and the keys must be set in both. Consider disableSkillShellExecution to blunt shell execution inside any locally added skill that does still load.
